replies.text:
Top Agricultural Exporters by Volume (Tonnes) – FAO 2023

🇧🇷 Brazil: 180.0M tonnes

🇺🇸 United States: 150.4M tonnes

🇨🇦 Canada: 63.4M tonnes

🇺🇦 Ukraine: 60.4M tonnes

🇦🇺 Australia: 56.8M tonnes

🇷🇺 Russia: 53.7M tonnes

🇦🇷 Argentina: 42.9M tonnes

🇫🇷 France: 42.8M tonnes

🇳🇱 Netherlands: 36.6M tonnes

🇮🇩 Indonesia: 35.6M tonnes

Why the Netherlands' "#2 Food Exporter" Claim is Misleading

While the Netherlands ranks 2nd in financial value ($100B+), it drops to 9th in actual volume. Here is why the "$2 exporter" title is PR statistical cherry-picking:

High Value vs. Real Volume: The Netherlands exports high-margin products (flowers, cheese, beer), while giants like Brazil and the US move heavy bulk commodities (grain, soy, meat) that feed the planet.

The Re-export Loophole: Home to Rotterdam, Europe's largest port, much of its export value consists of foreign goods (e.g., cocoa, fruit) passing through for processing or repackaging, artificially inflating export figures.

Size Narrative: Calling itself #2 creates an impressive "David vs. Goliath" story for a tiny nation, obscuring its reliance on import-export logistics rather than massive farm production.

comments.author: @vinspad3
comments.text:
3:40 yup. Re-exports. Without re-exports, the Dutch would rank 5th or 6th.

And if we ranked by tonnage not dollar, they'd fall to about 15th to 20th. The Dutch focus on high value exports due to their small usable land usage: luxury foods like cocoa instead of wheat like you mentioned.

If we ranked by both tonnage and only national exports (not re-export), it would fall even farther - 25th to 35th.

I love the geopolitical reasons for this. Most of Germany's major hubs are actually closer to Netherlands than they are to northern German cities, and the close Italian ports are blocked by the Alps, so Germany wants Dutch exports due to geography.

And because of France's tax policies and highly fragmented regional infrastructure, they arent able to keep up with the Dutch who have done a better job of collectively improving logistics nation-wide.

So they buy imports from less developed countries that dont have the production infrastructure, doubled down on processing, and re-export semi-processed goods to 'finishers.' So the cocoa beans get imported from Ivory Coast, get processed in Netherlands, then re-shipped to Germany and Austria to luxury chocolatiers.

Same with soybeans, sugar cane, coffee beans.

They created an industry around being the middle man. Brilliant!

replies.author: @GeographyEffect
replies.text: Exactly, the “middleman” role is a huge part of the story. The Netherlands combines high-value domestic production with ports, processing, and unusually direct access to Germany and the Rhine corridor, which lets it add value to goods produced far beyond Dutch farmland.

replies.author: @FabioT.
replies.text:
​@timothykeith1367 They are extremely efficient at producing vegetables, harvesting continuously for 10 months a year, or 10 to 12 times depending on the crop. However, these crops are low in calories and protein—they do not feed the world on their own. Tomatoes, for example, are 90 to 95% water. They are remarkably efficient at growing them, and these are essential foods, but we need to put everything into context: the pros and the cons. Otherwise, we risk spreading misinformation. Producing one ton of dry soybeans, cocoa, or coffee is a completely different challenge than producing one ton of tomatoes. 
18-19 million metric tons of food come from meat, milk, cheese, and eggs. To produce and feed all of this, 80-85% of their feed imports come from Brazil, Argentina, and the USA.

replies.text:
The Netherlands produces roughly three times as many agricultural products as it needs for domestic consumption. Around 75% of Dutch agricultural production is therefore destined for export.

The Port of Rotterdam is not the only important part of this export system. Schiphol Airport is at least as important, with its extensive international network. Every day, KLM aircraft fly to destinations all over the world, carrying fresh flowers, meat, vegetables and other agricultural products in their cargo holds.

Speed is particularly important when it comes to flowers. Dutch flowers, for example, may need to be delivered to a flower shop in the United States or Japan within 24 to 48 hours of being harvested. The Dutch agricultural sector therefore benefits greatly from KLM’s extensive global network, with daily flights to major destinations in Europe, North America, Asia and other parts of the world.

As a result, the Netherlands has not only developed a highly efficient agricultural sector, but also a logistics network capable of distributing these products rapidly around the world. It is precisely this combination of advanced agricultural technology, and Schiphol Airport and KLM’s international network that has helped make the Netherlands one of the world’s leading agricultural exporters.

"No oil money to spray green across a desert."

Is this video presenter really that ignorant or is he being intentionally dishonest?  The entire system of modern Dutch farming was built on a fire hose of natural gas money and associated cheap energy.  Exxon discovered one of the largest natural gas fields in the world near the northern coast of the Netherlands shortly after World War II.  That natural gas paid for not merely the rebuilding of the Netherlands post-war but its fundamental reconstruction.  This is the natural gas that displaced the coal upon which industrial Germany was originally built, and the development of the North Sea as a major global oil and gas province began with the following of geological trends to find further massive gas reserves further and further offshore in the 1960s.  German dependence on Russian natural gas developed as the super-massive Dutch natural gas reserves depleted.

replies.author: @gopher27
replies.text:
@jannetteberends8730 There were huge outlays of money in the mid-1960s.  The consolidation of Dutch farms into significantly larger productive units and the massive application of capital was a phenomenon of the 1960s.

😜
https://www.youtube.com/shorts/MB33RsyQE0I

I believe that the firm was acquired and consolidated at some point around 1980, but there used to exist an American company called Louisiana Land and Exploration.  In the late 1960s and early 1970s, it was grouped with some other high performing American stocks under the label "The Nifty Fifty", which has since been reapplied to Indian stocks.

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nifty_Fifty

The genesis of Louisiana Land and Exploration was that a Dutch farmer with the backing of some Dutch investors went to southern Louisiana and bought up 600,000 acres of swamp land for presumably pennies per acre.  They then spent huge sums of money building Dutch style dikes and sea walls with the aim of profitably applying "advanced" Dutch farming techniques on cheap American land.  The project turned into a cataclysmic disaster on par with Fordlandia and the Jari Project in the Brazilian Amazon.  The first hurricane to hit South Louisiana washed out all of the flood control infrastructure.

I believe that the original promoter ended up managing to hold on to administrative control as the equity investors were all wiped out and the debt was defaulted on.  Ultimately, huge volumes of oil and gas were discovered under the 600,000 acres of South Louisiana bayou country, and the promoter's children ended up extraordinarily wealthy.

I just mention this to highlight that Dutch agricultural "infrastructure" and "technology" has always existed.  However, the consolidation of farms and mechanization in the form of tractors and milking machines were phenomena of the 1960s rather than the 1950s.
